channel.title: Medical Xpress - latest medical and health news stories
channel.description: Medical Xpress internet news portal provides the latest news on science including: Physics, Nanotechnology, Life Sciences, Space Science, Earth Science, Environment, Health and Medicine.

item.title: Heterogeneity in breast cancer linked to risk of metastasis and treatment response
item.description: Differences within breast tumors and between patients are associated with the risk of metastasis and response to endocrine therapy, according to a new doctoral thesis from Karolinska Institutet. The findings also highlight the importance of long-term follow-up in capturing the full benefit of treatment.

item.title: Could the way we walk give clues about our mental health?
item.description: Experts in kinesiology and sport sciences and psychology from the University of Miami are collaborating on research to find out whether the way people walk could give clues about their mental health. The two researchers are exploring this question through a project called MindStep, where participants answer survey questions about their mental health and then complete different intellectual tasks while walking, as specialized cameras record and measure their walking patterns.

item.title: Tracking rising autism and ADHD diagnoses across Japan
item.description: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) are increasingly diagnosed in Japan, and the rise is no longer limited to children. National data show that adult ADHD diagnoses have overtaken ASD diagnoses, while young adult women have experienced a distinct increase. These trends may reflect greater awareness and changing diagnostic practices, rather than increased prevalence.

item.title: Scientists turn protein-making errors in cancer cells into a targeted kill switch
item.description: Like every other cell in the human body, cancer cells also produce their own share of proteins for survival. During this production process, cells often encounter a glitch called ribosomal frameshifting. This exceptionally rare event occurs roughly once in every 100,000 translation events, when the ribosome, while reading genetic instructions to make a protein, shifts its reading position. A recent Nature study investigated whether this protein-building glitch in cancer cells can be turned into a targeted cancer therapy.

item.title: The brain's 'dimmer switch' could help explain why attention drifts
item.description: McGill researchers have discovered that serotonin, a brain chemical best known for its role in mood and mental health, also helps regulate attention. "Our findings suggest serotonin-producing neurons deep in the midbrain act like a dimmer switch on attention," said Arjun Krishnaswamy, associate professor in the Department of Physiology, who co-led the study with associate professor Erik Cook. The findings were published in Nature Communications.

item.title: Organizations call for rapid, team-based endovascular hemorrhage control in trauma care
item.description: The American College of Surgeons (ACS) Committee on Trauma and the Society of Interventional Radiology (SIR) have issued a joint position statement reaffirming the role of interventional radiologists on multidisciplinary trauma teams and the importance of establishing reliable systems for rapid endovascular hemorrhage control in trauma situations.

item.title: AI assesses what really matters to people in health care—well-being
item.description: Artificial intelligence is helping to analyze and improve health care systems—from waiting times to treatment outcomes and costs. However, some of the most important aspects of care remain harder to measure—such as whether people feel heard, understood and genuinely cared for.

item.title: Early trial results suggest potential new treatment for stiff person syndrome
item.description: A multicenter clinical trial evaluating chimeric antigen receptor-T cell therapy (CAR-T cell therapy) for stiff person syndrome (SPS), a rare autoimmune neurologic disorder, has produced promising early results.

item.title: US youths see nearly 4,000 food marketing messages on digital media each year
item.description: U.S. children and adolescents see thousands of food marketing messages on digital media platforms each year, according to new research published in JAMA Pediatrics. And 92% of the marketed food and beverage products are considered unhealthy.

item.title: It takes a neighborhood to keep kids active
item.description: Getting youngsters to go outside and play doesn't just rely on family support, but also on a neighborhood coming together to create a good environment, University of Alberta research shows.

item.title: Two-year study will examine how gender-affirming hormone therapy affects energy use and blood vessel function
item.description: The research team at the LeiCeM Cluster of Excellence is preparing a new study. It builds on the first phase of the Hormones and Health study (HHS), in which researchers from the Helmholtz Institute for Metabolic, Obesity and Vascular Research (HI-MAG), Leipzig University and the University of Leipzig Medical Center followed trans people undergoing gender-affirming hormone therapy. The second cohort will be studied over a period of two years, with the study expected to begin in early 2027.

item.title: Study challenges long-held fears about overactive bladder drugs and dementia
item.description: New research published in JAMA Network Open finds anticholinergic medications, commonly prescribed for overactive bladder (OAB), may not increase dementia risk after all compared to beta-3 agonists, the newer drug class that has been presumed to be safer for the brain.

item.title: Cluster headache linked to pronounced levels of burnout symptoms
item.description: People with cluster headache often experience more than intense pain. A new study from Karolinska Institutet, published in Headache, suggests that many also report symptoms of burnout and exhaustion, particularly during periods when headache attacks are frequent. The findings underline the importance of addressing sleep, recovery and daily functioning as part of patient care.

item.title: Why obesity affects males and females differently
item.description: University of California, Riverside, scientists have an explanation for why males and females respond differently to obesity. They report in PNAS Nexus that certain immune cell populations in fat tissue may protect against obesity-related inflammation while others may contribute to harmful metabolic changes. They found these immune cells, called eosinophils and traditionally associated with asthma and allergies, behave differently in males and females.

item.title: Your brain may map emotional concepts onto a hexagonal grid, new study suggests
item.description: Everyday life throws a whole range of emotional experiences our way, from exciting and relaxing moments to tense or gloomy encounters. Each experience is shaped by what's present around us in the moment, the sensations our body is experiencing and our past experiences. This entire scene is set by the brain, which draws on these experiences of the past, organizing the information it gathers into mental maps that help us predict what might happen and respond appropriately to different situations.

item.title: In phase 2 trial, novel therapy significantly reduced triglyceride levels
item.description: A phase 2b clinical trial led by Mass General Brigham Heart and Vascular Institute researchers shows that a monoclonal antibody therapy called MAR001 can significantly reduce triglyceride levels within 12 weeks for patients with high triglyceride levels. Their results are published in the New England Journal of Medicine and were presented simultaneously at the American Heart Association's annual meeting.

item.title: Childhood cancers may spread by 'shape-shifting' rather than mutating
item.description: Researchers at the University of East Anglia (UK) have proposed an explanation for why some childhood tumors spread aggressively around the body despite having relatively few genetic faults. For years, experts believed cancers become more dangerous by accumulating genetic mutations that allow them to invade new tissues and evade treatment. But a new paper shows how childhood cancers may not always need extra mutations to spread.

item.title: Magnetic fields can revive intracellular transport in ALS
item.description: A study led by cell biologist Dr. Arun Pal at the HZDR, in collaboration with research partners in Dresden and Rostock, has found that electromagnetic alternating fields can partially reverse key pathological changes in human nerve cells. The finding has been published in the journal Cells.

item.title: Cleaner bedroom air may help manage blood sugar in prediabetes
item.description: Using portable filters to reduce exposure to air pollution during sleep may stabilize the large spikes in blood sugar experienced by people with prediabetes, a condition in which sugar (glucose) levels are higher than normal, a new study shows.

item.title: Concussion study upends understanding of what makes head impacts dangerous
item.description: Concussions—essentially mild traumatic brain injuries—are among the most common injuries sustained on athletic fields. In the U.S., an estimated 3.8 million sports-related concussions occur every year. But new research by Stanford Medicine scientists and collaborators suggests that the prevailing understanding of the forces that lead to concussion may be missing the mark.

item.title: Experimental mRNA therapy promotes repair after heart attack damage
item.description: Scientists have developed a treatment that 'reawakens' heart muscle cells so they start to divide and help repair damaged muscle.

item.title: AI predicts PTSD risk based on stories about what brought patients to the emergency room
item.description: An AI tool can analyze patients' narratives about injuries that sent them to the emergency room to predict who will later develop posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), a new study found.

item.title: Could a plant metabolite act as a natural sunscreen to help prevent skin cancer?
item.description: Research in Photochemistry and Photobiology indicates that a plant metabolite that can block the effects of ultraviolet (UV) light has promising potential as a natural sunscreen when applied to human skin.

item.title: Cancer clinical trial participants reimbursed a median $2,128 for nonmedical expenses
item.description: New research reveals that participating in cancer clinical trials can cause financial burdens that are shaped by both socioeconomic and logistical factors. The analysis published by Wiley online in CANCER, indicates the need for better reimbursement programs to improve equitable access to, and retention in, cancer clinical trials.

item.title: Aspirin does not prevent recurrence after treatment for colorectal cancer liver metastases
item.description: Colorectal cancer is one of the most common cancers in Norway, which also has one of the highest incidence rates in the world.

item.title: Microbiome therapy shows promise for preventing deadly bloodstream infections in early trial
item.description: Researchers at City of Hope and collaborators have pioneered a new approach to preventing dangerous bloodstream infections in patients receiving donor stem cell transplants for blood cancers. The first-of-its-kind therapy delivers 16 carefully selected beneficial bacteria designed to restore the microbiome and fight harmful pathogens.

item.title: Experimental weight-loss drug eases painful knee osteoarthritis in two clinical trials
item.description: For people with painful knee osteoarthritis (OA) who are overweight or have obesity, everyday activities such as walking, climbing stairs and standing up from a chair can be difficult. In two Northwestern University–led Phase III clinical trials involving more than 1,000 participants combined, those taking the highest dose of retatrutide, a new experimental weight-loss injectable drug, lost about one-quarter of their body weight on average.

item.title: Single iron infusion improved exercise capacity in people with the most common form of heart failure
item.description: A new study by investigators from the Mass General Brigham Heart and Vascular Institute found that a single iron infusion improved exercise capacity in people with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) and iron deficiency. The findings suggest that replenishing iron could help address the physical limitations associated with this condition. Results were presented at the 2026 American Heart Association Scientific Sessions and published simultaneously in Circulation.

item.title: Financial incentives nearly double quit rates among underserved people who smoke in national study
item.description: Offering financial incentives to people trying to quit smoking nearly doubled cessation rates among medically underserved adults undergoing lung cancer screening, according to a large national clinical trial involving Henry Ford Health.

item.title: Potential driver of severe early-onset preeclampsia identified
item.description: Severe early-onset preeclampsia has confounded doctors for more than 2,000 years. It can strike as early as 20 weeks into pregnancy, sending blood pressure soaring and putting both the mother and baby at risk.
